passage: Oakwood Middle School Library Club invites all students and families to the Spring Book Swap on Saturday, April 12, from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. in the school gym. Bring up to five gently used books to trade. For each book you bring, you will receive one ticket, and each ticket can be exchanged for a different book on the day. Books that are torn or have missing pages cannot be accepted. Students who bring more than five books may donate the extras to the club, and the club will give them to the children's hospital. Free lemonade will be served, and volunteers from the Library Club will be wearing yellow shirts to help you find books. No money is needed to attend. If you have questions, please email Ms. Alvarez at the library.

passage: Mina stood on the porch, patting every pocket of her jacket. The key was gone. Her parents would not be home until six, and the wind was growing colder by the minute. She remembered kicking a soccer ball at the park after school, and she hurried back along the sidewalk, her eyes fixed on the ground. At the park, the grass was empty except for an old man feeding pigeons. "Did you see a key?" she asked. He smiled and pointed with his cane toward the bench. There, glinting in the afternoon sun, lay the key on a small silver ring. Mina laughed with relief and thanked him twice. As she walked home, she made a promise to herself: from now on, the key would stay zipped inside her backpack.
stem: Why did Mina go back to the park?
choices: The old man had called her name.
Her parents told her to look there.
She wanted to feed the pigeons.
explanation: She recalled kicking a soccer ball at the park.

passage: An octopus has no shell and no bones, yet it survives in waters full of hungry predators. Its best defense is camouflage. Special cells in its skin, called chromatophores, can expand or shrink in a fraction of a second. Each cell holds a tiny sac of color, so the octopus can turn from red to brown to nearly white as it moves across a reef. Some octopuses also change the texture of their skin, raising small bumps to look like rough rocks or seaweed. Scientists once believed the animal relied on its eyes to match its surroundings. However, recent studies suggest that the skin itself may sense light, helping the octopus blend in even when parts of its body are hidden from view. If camouflage fails, the octopus can squirt a cloud of dark ink and escape.

choices: The octopus uses color and texture changes to protect itself.
The octopus is the fastest animal in the sea.
The octopus builds shells from rocks.
The octopus can only live near a reef.
explanation: Most of the passage describes how the octopus camouflages itself.

passage: Beginning more than two thousand years ago, a network of trade routes known as the Silk Road linked China with the lands around the Mediterranean Sea. Few merchants traveled the entire distance. Instead, goods passed from trader to trader, and each handoff raised the price. Silk, spices, and paper moved westward, while glass, gold, and horses traveled east. Yet merchandise was not the only thing that crossed these deserts and mountains. Ideas, religions, and even diseases moved along the same paths. Buddhism, for instance, spread from India into East Asia largely through travelers on these roads. Towns along the way, such as Samarkand, grew wealthy by providing food, water, and shelter to caravans. Historians therefore describe the Silk Road not merely as a place for buying and selling but as a meeting point of cultures.
stem: Why did goods become more expensive as they traveled along the Silk Road?
choices: Thieves destroyed most of the cargo.
Governments banned silk from being sold.
Each trader who handled them raised the price.
Merchants had to pay to cross the sea.
explanation: The passage says each handoff raised the price.

passage: Dear Families, Beginning next month, Harbor Middle School will move to a split lunch schedule. At present, all 600 students eat together at 12:15, which creates long lines and leaves many students with only ten minutes to finish their meals. Under the new plan, sixth and seventh graders will eat at 11:45, and eighth graders will eat at 12:30. The change will not shorten any class, but some periods will begin five minutes later. Teachers have already adjusted their lesson plans. We understand that some students will miss eating with friends in other grades. To address this concern, the cafeteria will host a monthly Friday lunch when all grades may sit together. We believe the new system will make lunchtime calmer and give everyone enough time to eat. Please contact the office with questions. Sincerely, Principal Okafor

explanation: The letter cites long lines and only ten minutes to eat.

passage: Every spring, Grandfather Chen knelt in the same corner of the yard and pressed a handful of seeds into the soil as gently as if he were tucking in a baby. Lian, who was nine, thought it was a strange habit, since the store sold tomatoes all year. "Those are not the same tomatoes," he told her one morning, wiping his hands on his old gray apron. "These seeds came from my mother's garden in Hangzhou. She gave them to me the day I left." Lian looked at the tiny brown specks with new respect. That summer, she watered the plants every evening without being asked, and when the first tomato turned red, she carried it to her grandfather in both hands. He did not say anything at first; he only held it up to the light, and his eyes shone.
stem: Why does Grandfather Chen plant these seeds every spring?
choices: They grow faster than store seeds.
They connect him to his mother and his old home.
He wants to sell tomatoes at the market.
Lian asked him to start a garden.
explanation: The seeds came from his mother's garden in Hangzhou.

passage: When a honeybee finds a rich patch of flowers, she returns to the hive and performs a figure-eight dance on the honeycomb. The straight middle part of the dance, called the waggle run, carries the message. The angle of the run, measured against gravity, tells the other bees which direction to fly relative to the sun. The length of the run indicates distance: the longer the waggle, the farther the flowers. Researchers who first decoded the dance in the 1940s were astonished, because it suggested that insects could share precise information symbolically. Later experiments strengthened that view. When scientists moved a food source while a hive's dancers were advertising its old location, bees that followed the dance arrived at the empty spot and searched there, which showed that they were relying on the dancers' directions rather than simply smelling the food.
stem: What does the length of the waggle run tell other bees?
choices: How far away the flowers are
explanation: The passage says a longer waggle means farther flowers.

passage: Before canals, farmers in inland regions often struggled to sell their crops. Wagons were slow, roads turned to mud in the rain, and a heavy load of grain could cost nearly as much to haul as it was worth. Then a canal was dug linking the interior to the coast. Barges pulled by mules carried goods for a fraction of the price, and shipping times dropped from weeks to days. Towns along the waterway grew into busy markets, and farmers began planting crops specifically to sell rather than only to feed their families. Within a generation, however, railroads arrived and were faster still. Many canals fell out of use, and some towns that had boomed began to shrink.
stem: Why did farmers have trouble selling crops before the canal?
choices: Moving crops by wagon was slow and costly.
Few people wanted to buy grain.
Farmers had no land to plant on.
explanation: Wagons were slow and hauling could cost almost as much as the crop was worth.

passage: Leaves look green in summer because they contain chlorophyll, a pigment that captures sunlight for making food. As days grow shorter in autumn, trees stop producing chlorophyll, and the green fades. The yellow and orange colors that remain were present all along; they were simply hidden. Red leaves are different. Their color comes from anthocyanins, pigments that many trees manufacture only in autumn, from sugars trapped in the leaves. Bright, sunny days and cool nights produce the richest reds, because sunshine builds up sugar while cold prevents it from leaving the leaf. In a cloudy, warm autumn, the display is usually duller. Brown leaves, finally, result from waste products left behind after the other pigments are gone.

choices: Trees make them from sunlight in October.

They show once the green chlorophyll fades.
They are produced from trapped sugars.
explanation: Those colors were present all along but hidden by chlorophyll.

stem: Puppy is to dog as kitten is to ___
explanation: A puppy is a young dog and a kitten is a young cat.

explanation: Hot and cold are opposites, as are up and down.

stem: Hand is to glove as foot is to ___
explanation: A glove covers a hand as a sock covers a foot.

stem: Teacher is to school as doctor is to ___
explanation: A teacher works at a school; a doctor works at a hospital.

stem: Pencil is to write as scissors is to ___
explanation: A pencil is used to write; scissors are used to cut.

stem: Sculptor is to statue as architect is to ___
explanation: A sculptor creates statues; an architect designs buildings.

stem: Scarce is to plentiful as ancient is to ___
explanation: Scarce and plentiful are opposites, as are ancient and modern.

stem: Thermometer is to temperature as ruler is to ___
explanation: A thermometer measures temperature; a ruler measures length.

stem: Fish is to school as wolf is to ___

stem: Frugal is to wasteful as cautious is to ___

stem: Verbose is to concise as lavish is to ___
